name: West Face

ways.name: Lake outlet climbers' path into the west cirque
ways.season: mid-Jul-Sep, once the gully and cirque talus are snow-free
ways.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for about 2.25 miles with a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek near the 1.5-mile mark, then left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, a second log crossing, and steep rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about four miles and 2,280 ft, an hour and three quarters to two hours for a fit party carrying a rack.

The shorter of the two ways into the west cirque starts at the lake outlet, at the north end below the small dam. Cross there and follow a well-cairned climbers' path across the timbered hillside; it gains height quickly and deposits you on the talus field under the west face. Reckon about an hour from the lake, plus twenty to twenty-five minutes of boulder-hopping to reach the wall itself.

This is the way parties who have been there recommend, and it is the one to take unless the outlet crossing is unreasonable.

Colchuck Lake is the last water. The cirque and the route are dry.

ways.name: Southern line via the Aasgard-side slopes and the leftmost gully
ways.season: mid-Jul-Sep; the gully holds snow into early summer
ways.notes:
The alternative when you do not want to cross the outlet. Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, then cut north through a band of slide alder — look for cairns, because this is a genuine bushwhack — and climb the leftmost gully about 1,000 ft to its top. From there contour east on easy ground into the cirque.

An hour and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line and a lot more brush, but no ford. A winter/spring variation on the same idea follows a steepening gully starting near the lake's southwest edge.

In a heavy year the gully holds snow well into early summer and an axe or light traction is worth having.

priorPrimaryResearch: v0 notes say the outlet line is what parties who have been there recommend; paragraph describes both options.

name: Colchuck Glacier

ways.name: Colchuck Lake, snow-covered glacier (early season)
ways.season: Jun-early Jul, while the glacier is well filled and crevasses stay bridged
ways.notes:
Stuart Lake Trail #1599 from the FR 7601 road end for about 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.6 miles of steep switchbacks through boulders to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Call it four miles and 2,200 ft. This is the last reliable water.

Follow the boot path along the east shore to the inlet at the south end, then leave the trail. Gain the crest of the lateral moraine as early as you can — the alternative is a long session in genuinely loose scree and talus, and parties consistently report an hour of boulder-hopping through it when they stay low.

With good snow cover much of this basin, and later much of the glacier, can be glissaded on the way out, which is why parties favour the early window. Aim to be off the glacier before early afternoon: it softens badly and post-holing plus wet-slide potential make a late descent both slow and unpleasant.

ways.name: Colchuck Lake, bare-ice glacier (late season)
ways.season: Aug-Sep, once the glacier has opened up and gone to bare, sun-cupped ice
ways.notes:
The walk to Colchuck Lake and up the moraine is the same, and easier without snow. What changes is everything above the moraine.

By August the glacier typically melts out to hard, sun-cupped ice. It is not heavily crevassed, but crevasses and marginal moats that were bridged in June are open, and the surface no longer takes a boot step. Crampons and an axe stop being optional and a rope becomes a real consideration for the margins.

The scree and talus below the moraine is at its loosest now, and rockfall off the surrounding walls is more frequent with no snow holding things in place. The glissade descent is gone — plan on down-climbing everything you came up, which is the main reason the day gets longer.

priorPrimaryResearch: Same approach in both variants (seasonal split of glacier condition); early-season snow is the classic window for the Colchuck Glacier, so index 0 is reasonable.

name: North Face

ways.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
ways.notes:
Identical to the Beckey Route walk-in, which is why the two are so often climbed on the same day. Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass; about 1.75 miles of maintained trail to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream, marked with a large cairn; then the climbers' path up slabs, talus and heather into the bowl below the towers and up the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft.

In the gully, staying climber's left for the lower two thirds and then crossing to climber's right keeps you on the most stable ground.

ways.name: Early-season snow to the notch
ways.notes:
Same line, but the gully feeding the Liberty Bell-Concord notch holds snow into late June most years and the boot path lower down may still be buried. Ice axe standard, crampons if it has refrozen.

One upside of the early season here: while the gully is snow-filled the rock in it is locked in place, and rockfall gets noticeably worse once it melts out.

SR-20 is closed across Washington Pass every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so this window begins whenever the highway reopens.

priorPrimaryResearch: Variant 1 is the same Blue Lake line under early-season snow; the prose describes the summer walk (variant 0) with a note about early snow in the gully.

ways.name: Holden Village and the Copper Creek boot trail to the Copper Basin bench
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, best in August; the snowfield below the ridge often still wants crampons and an axe into July
ways.notes:
There is no drivable trailhead. Ferry from Chelan or Field's Point to Lucerne, shuttle up to Holden Village near 3,300 ft. Both have been closed since the December 2025 flood and landslide.

From the village, walk the old mine road and Railroad Creek Trail about half a mile east to a large tailings pile around 3,320 ft, where the Copper Creek Trail branches off on the far side of the creek. A footbridge is the normal crossing; if it is out this becomes a ford and it runs highest in early season.

Above the tailings the boot trail turns steep at once, climbing about 0.7 mile of open burned hillside — loose footing in standing dead timber, unmaintained, slower than its half-mile suggests — before dropping into the Copper Creek drainage. It then parallels the creek south about three miles to an open bench at roughly 5,600 ft, which is the standard camp. Maps show maintained tread ending near 4,750 ft but the boot path continues; do not read the end of the mapped trail as the end of the path.

From camp, ford Copper Creek to its west side and climb into the upper basin on talus and slabs, following the outlet stream that drains the glacier remnant on the peak's east face.

ways.name: Phelps Creek over Spider Gap
ways.notes: From the Phelps Creek trailhead, walk up through Spider Meadow and the Spider Glacier to Spider Gap, drop past the Lyman Glacier to Lyman Lake, then follow the Railroad Creek trail down the valley to Copper Creek. It avoids the boat and shuttle but is far longer, with a steep snow climb to the gap.

name: Standard Route (Southeast Ridge via Jackita Ridge / Crater Lake Trail)

ways.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Jackita Ridge #738 and the Crater Lake trail #746
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Oct; the Canyon Creek ford is the constraint in spring and early summer
ways.notes: Park at the Canyon Creek trailhead at about 1,900 ft on Highway 20 near milepost 141, roughly fifty-five miles west of Winthrop or thirty-three east of Marblemount. Vault toilet, no drinking water. There is no bridge over Canyon Creek on Jackita Ridge trail #738, and the Forest Service describes the crossing as difficult and potentially hazardous in spring and early summer. How people get across changes from year to year — one season a shin-deep wade a hundred yards upstream, another a log fifty metres up — so do not plan on a fixed method. The first mile and a half is brushy. The trail then climbs steeply through timber on a long series of switchbacks to the junction with the Crater Lake trail #746. That junction is unsigned, reported by two separate parties, and its elevation is published as either 5,000 or 5,260 ft. Turn onto #746 and climb toward Crater Lake. There is a second unmarked junction just before the lake, leading to the old east lookout site; stay with the main path, which runs along the south shore. Crater Lake is the last water — the ground above is dry, and the lake itself is shallow enough that water filtered at the outlet comes out warm. The whole peak is commonly given as fourteen to fifteen miles round trip with about 6,300 ft of gain.

ways.name: Devils Dome loop from the East Bank trailhead
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, as a multi-day trip
ways.notes:
A genuinely different approach with a specific purpose: it exists to avoid the Canyon Creek ford. The party who wrote it up said so directly, having judged a day trip from Canyon Creek to involve a difficult crossing at the time they were there.

It starts from the East Bank trailhead near Ruby Creek and runs roughly forty-eight miles with about 13,100 ft of gain over three days, taking in Devils Dome. That is a very different undertaking from the day-trip standard, and it is chosen for access rather than for the mountain.

Nothing is published on a Granite Creek or East Creek approach, so do not assume one exists.

priorPrimaryResearch: Paragraph is the Canyon Creek / Jackita Ridge #738 / Crater Lake trail approach (v0), the day-trip standard; v1 Devils Dome loop exists only to avoid the ford. proseClosest=1 is a word-overlap artefact.

ways.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack cable car and Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass, then over the Challenger Glacier and through West Challenger Notch
ways.season: Jun-Sep. The Crooked Thumb Glacier itself can be severely crevassed with open moats late in the season
ways.notes:
From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, the Hannegan Pass Trail runs about 4 miles and 2,500 ft to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, then drops off the north side into the Chilliwack River valley and loses most of the gain again.

The valley traverse passes Copper Creek Camp around mile 9 and U.S. Cabin Camp around mile 12; expect brushy tread near U.S. Cabin and, in blowdown years, real timber. One party logged roughly two hours to move 1.5 miles through fallen trunks beyond the cable-car crossing. The Chilliwack is crossed on a hand-pulled cable car, which is mandatory and somewhat exposed; the river is not reliably fordable.

Beyond it the Brush Creek Trail climbs to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, roughly 17 miles in. From Whatcom Camp, leave trail and traverse below Whatcom Peak's northeast flank on the Whatcom Glacier to Perfect Pass, about 4.5 hours and 1,750 ft. Perfect Pass has reliable running water and is a common high camp. From there rope up, climb the Challenger Glacier to a high bench near 8,100 ft, and descend through West Challenger Notch onto the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Round trip is on the order of 40 miles.

ways.name: Big Beaver valley and Wiley Ridge
ways.notes: Take the water taxi from Ross Lake Resort to the Big Beaver landing and follow the Big Beaver trail up the valley toward Luna Camp. Leave the trail and climb Wiley Ridge off-trail to the basin on its south side, then continue to the Challenger Arm and cross to West Challenger Notch above the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Expect several days and serious bushwhacking.

name: Dark Glacier Route

ways.name: Swamp Creek climbers' path to the col
ways.season: Early to mid summer gives firm, well-bridged snow with least crevasse danger; by late summer more crevasses are open and the glacier is less stable.
ways.notes: This is the line most descriptions still call standard, and it is the brushy one. From the road end at the bridge, follow the crest trail south to the first creekside camp and on to the camp at the Swamp Creek fork. Leave the maintained trail there for the long-abandoned climbers' path: cross Swamp Creek on a large log to its east side and force about a quarter mile of dense slide alder and vine maple. Above that a headwall bars the basin; the way up it is at the far left, and the route then climbs steep forest, veering right at the end to a natural saddle around 5,040 ft. Beyond lies a further, higher basin near 5,500 ft below the slabs of the receding glacier.

ways.name: Crest trail to Hemlock Camp and the northwest climb
ways.season: Early to mid summer for the best glacier conditions, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
ways.notes: The newer variant continues farther south on the crest trail, roughly to the Hemlock camp, then leaves the trail and climbs northwest through open forest and slopes — about 3,500 ft of gain — to reach the glacier from the ridge above. It avoids nearly all of the Swamp Creek brush and is substantially easier ground, even though the Swamp Creek line is still the one usually called standard. It is the better choice for a party that wants to arrive with something left, and it is what the far side of the ridge separating this peak from its neighbour gives access to.

priorPrimaryResearch: Variant 0's own notes say Swamp Creek is still what most descriptions call standard; Mountaineers TRs report Hemlock Camp is gone to beetle-kill deadfall and the Dark Fin Col climb is choked with deadfall. Prose lays out both options explicitly.

name: Direct North Buttress

ways.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
ways.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
ways.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, where a hand-pulled cable car carries hikers over in high water (by late July and August the river is often below knee deep and can be forded), then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since the 2021 fire.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.

ways.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
ways.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
ways.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and follows an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.

priorPrimaryResearch: Hannegan Pass to the Chilliwack is the standard US approach to Bear Mountain. The Canadian side needs a legal border crossing and an overgrown tread. The paragraph describes the Hannegan line.

name: Dome Glacier

ways.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek route
ways.notes:
From the Suiattle River Road, take the Downey Creek Trail on the east bank through old growth — about six and a half miles to the Six Mile campsite at roughly 2,440 ft. The maintained trail effectively ends there.

The Bachelor Creek route continues on the north side of the creek and crosses to the south at about 4,000 ft on a log; some parties cross higher, nearer 4,400. Between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft the tread is genuinely overgrown — parties describe swimming through brush without being able to see their feet — but the important point is that the trail IS still there under it, so do not abandon it and start making your own line. At about 4,500 ft an old avalanche swath from 2002 wiped out the trail and this is the hardest stretch to get through.

Above that, cross the pass at about 5,900 ft north-west of Cub Lake and descend to the lake at 5,338 ft, around fourteen miles in. Good camping. A well-established trail then crosses flats and climbs heather beside a cascade to Itswoot Ridge at about 6,200 ft, which is the better-placed camp for summit day. Reported car-to-camp times have been nine to eleven hours; this is a multi-day approach, not a hike-in.

ways.name: Ptarmigan Traverse from Cascade Pass
ways.notes: Dome Peak is the far end of the Ptarmigan Traverse, so it is also reached from the Cascade Pass trailhead by travelling the whole traverse south. This is the long way in by a wide margin and is undertaken as part of the traverse rather than as an approach to the peak; parties heading only for Dome use the Downey Creek side.

priorPrimaryResearch: Variant 1 notes say parties heading only for Dome use the Downey Creek side; Ptarmigan Traverse is the long way. Prose describes Downey/Bachelor Creek.

ways.name: Bean Creek Trail to Earl Pass
ways.season: Class 2 on dry ground from July into October, and a popular spring snow climb before that, when an axe and sometimes crampons are wanted on the steep south-facing summit slopes.
ways.notes: From the road-end trailhead start north on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391, a mellow stretch of old roadbed beside Beverly Creek, and at the signed junction bear right and east onto the Bean Creek Trail; the Turnpike Trail carries straight on up the wrong valley for this peak. The Bean Creek tread climbs through forest into a tight, steep-sided valley, drops to a ford of Bean Creek, then keeps climbing until the forest breaks open into a broad flower meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats. That basin is the last dependable water. At the meadow fork bear right and east rather than left into the upper basin; tread goes intermittent through the upper meadows before switchbacking to a broad saddle on the divide.

ways.name: Standup Creek trail
ways.notes: From the Standup Creek trailhead, the trail runs up a gentle valley, then steepens through open hillside to the southwest ridge of Earl Peak, where a boot path leads to the summit. Quieter and gentler at first than the Bean Creek side, with the hard climbing saved for the upper slopes.

ways.name: Downey Creek, Bachelor Creek and Itswoot Ridge
ways.notes: From the Suiattle River Road, follow the Downey Creek trail up the valley, then turn up Bachelor Creek on a faint, brushy path toward Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge. From the ridge, cross the glaciers east toward the Gunsight Range. Plan on a long two-day approach.

ways.name: From Stehekin up Agnes and Spruce Creeks
ways.notes: From High Bridge on the Stehekin Valley Road, follow the Pacific Crest Trail south up Agnes Creek about ten miles to the Spruce Creek confluence, crossing both creeks on logs. Then go cross-country, through dense brush, up toward the Icy-Spruce col for a high camp facing the Gunsights. Reaching Stehekin takes a boat or floatplane, so this is a multi-day trip.

name: East Ridge

ways.name: The Kindy Creek roadbed and the ribbon-marked climbers' trail to the Point 5116 saddle
ways.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles to the signed forest road 1570 junction and turn right. Cross the river on a concrete bridge and continue about half a mile to a Y-junction where the right fork is blocked by boulders; park there, at roughly 1,150 to 1,300 ft, because a long-standing washout keeps most parties from driving higher.

A climbers' trail flagged with pink ribbon every fifty to a hundred and fifty feet leaves the old roadbed and climbs steeply and directly through old growth - about seventeen hundred vertical feet in its first mile, with few switchbacks - to a ridge saddle near Point 5116. From the saddle the route climbs roughly a thousand feet to Peak 5791, then traverses heather benches and meadows above the lake, crossing or contouring Peak 5860, to reach the base of the east ridge.

ways.name: Camping at the lake below the ridge
ways.notes: The lake below the ridge is the common overnight for this route and turns it from a very long day into a comfortable two. The camping is in the meadows on the lake's east side and there is reliable water. Parties doing it in a day still pass through the same ground and should treat the lake as the last water before the ridge.

priorPrimaryResearch: Only v0 is an approach (Kindy Creek roadbed and ribbon trail); v1 is a camping note on the same ground. Paragraph matches v0.
